title: Martha and Mary
hookLine: Martha is busy serving; Mary sits and listens, and Jesus says she chose the good part (Luke 10:38–42)

cards: "Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone?" That's Martha, in Luke's Gospel, and she has a point. Jesus has come to her village and she has opened her home.

There's a guest to feed, and a house to run. And her sister Mary is sitting on the floor at Jesus' feet, listening, not lifting a finger. She goes straight to the guest and asks him to send her sister in to help.
His answer is not the one she wants.

teach.b: Luke says Mary "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word," while "Martha was cumbered about much serving." Cumbered: weighed down, pulled in every direction.

Then the answer, gentle, her name said twice: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her."
First, notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't tell Martha that cooking is wrong, or that she should stop serving guests. He names the worry.
Second, the one thing. Luke doesn't spell it out. What the text shows is Mary sitting and hearing his word, and Christians usually read the one thing as that listening.
The King James says that good part; other English Bibles say the better part, which is where today's line comes from.

Third, Martha is not the villain. In John's Gospel, when her brother Lazarus has died, it's Martha who goes out to meet Jesus on the road and says, "I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God."

Some Christian writers have read the two sisters as two ways of life, active service and quiet prayer, and have argued about which matters more. Others say a life needs both, and that even Martha's kitchen can be holy.
Busy work fills every gap: the dishes, the inbox, the small urgent tasks that feel like duty.

teach.h: MARY HATH CHOSEN THAT GOOD PART.
teach.b: The story asks a quiet question: is there a better part you're too busy to sit down for?

how: Christians read Luke 10:38–42 as a call to make time to listen to God, and some retreat houses and prayer groups use Mary's sitting at Jesus' feet as a picture of quiet prayer.

games.q: you're Martha. the guest is here, the work is piling up, and your sister is sitting on the floor listening. what do you do?
o: keep working quietly and say nothing.
ask the guest to send your sister to help.
sit down beside her and let the meal wait.
games.why: Martha goes to Jesus and asks, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? he answers gently: Mary hath chosen that good part.

practice: For the next two minutes, be Mary: put down whatever you were about to do, and simply listen, to the sounds in the room, the sounds outside it, your own breath going in and out.
When you drift back into the kitchen, planning, tidying, answering, smile at Martha and come back to the floor. If you pray, this can be a time of listening in your own tradition's way.

wordCard.voice: Martha. The sister in Luke's Gospel busy serving in her kitchen, while Mary sat at Jesus' feet and heard his word. Today's word.

orig.note: the Greek word in Luke 10:42 behind 'part': a share or portion. Mary chose the good portion.
